summary: Defines binary formats for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selectors, which describe a particular flow of packets, for use with flow bindings in Mobile IPv6. A traffic selector lets a device say which traffic should be sent to which of its addresses. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Like sticky labels that say which kind of mail goes to which of your mailboxes, so a phone with several connections knows where each kind of traffic should arrive.

questions: what is a binary traffic selector
how does an ipv6 traffic selector match a flow label
what are ts format values 1 and 2
subtitle: Compact binary formats for describing a flow of IPv4 or IPv6 packets, used by Mobile IPv6 flow bindings.

tldr.problem: Flow bindings in Mobile IPv6 need a way to say which packets belong to a flow, so that a device can steer different traffic to different addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6088 defines two binary traffic selector formats, one for IPv4 (TS Format 1) and one for IPv6 (TS Format 2). A set of flags says which fields are present, and most fields have a start and an optional end value to describe a range.
tldr.outcome: The selectors identify flows efficiently from well-known IP and transport header fields. RFC 6088 only defines the formats; the sub-option itself is in RFC 6089.

today: RFC 6088 is a Proposed Standard and, per the metadata on this site, has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the formats for the traffic selector sub-option of RFC 6089.

sections.title: What a Binary Traffic Selector Is
sections.content:
RFC 6088 defines binary formats for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic selector sub-options, as introduced in RFC 6089 (flow bindings in Mobile IPv6 and NEMO Basic Support). The traffic selector format is meant to identify flows efficiently, based on well-known fields in IPv4, IPv6 and transport headers such as TCP and UDP.

All selectors in this document describe data packets sent from a corresponding node to the mobile node, as seen by the home agent. The source fields therefore name the correspondent node, and the destination fields name a registered home address of the mobile node.
sections.eli5: A traffic selector is a label that describes a kind of traffic, such as everything coming from one friend to one of your mailboxes.

sections.title: Sub-Option, TS Format and Flags
sections.content:
RFC 6089 defines the traffic selector sub-option. This RFC adds two values for its TS Format field: 1 for an IPv4 binary traffic selector and 2 for an IPv6 binary traffic selector.

In each format, a block of flag bits (A to N for IPv4, A to P for IPv6) shows which fields follow in the message. Most fields come in pairs: a Start value, and an optional End value that turns it into a range. An End field MUST NOT be included unless its Start field is, and the receiver matches every value between Start and End, inclusive.

The Reserved bits MUST be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. Each format also has an alignment requirement that depends on which flags are set, as shown for each format below.
sections.eli5: The label has a row of tick boxes at the top. Each box says whether a certain piece of information, like a sender or a port, is written below.

sections.title: The IPv4 Binary Traffic Selector
sections.content:
The IPv4 selector has fourteen flags, A to N, and these fields: Start and End Source Address (A, B), Start and End Destination Address (C, D), Start and End IPsec SPI (E, F), Start and End Source Port (G, H), Start and End Destination Port (I, J), Start and End DS (K, L) and Start and End Protocol (M, N). Addresses and SPIs are 32 bits, ports are 16 bits, and DS and protocol values are 8 bits.

Alignment is 4n if any of A to F is set, 2n if any of G to J is set, and n if any of K to N is set.

The DS field is called the Type of Service field in RFC 791. Following RFC 3260 and ECN (RFC 3168), the field here is 8 bits long, but the 6 most significant bits are the DS value to match and the 2 least significant bits MUST be ignored in any comparison. The IPsec SPI is defined in RFC 4303.
sections.eli5: For IPv4 the label can say who sent it, who it is for, a security tag, a door number (port), how urgent it is and what kind of traffic it is.

sections.title: The IPv6 Binary Traffic Selector
sections.content:
The IPv6 selector has sixteen flags, A to P. It has the same fields as the IPv4 one for addresses (128 bits each), SPI, ports, and the traffic class (TC) in place of DS, plus two new pairs: Start and End Flow Label (G, H), and Start and End Next Header (O, P) in place of Protocol.

Alignment is 8n if any of A to D is set, 4n if any of E to H is set, 2n if any of I to L is set, and n if any of M to P is set.

The flow label is 24 bits long in RFC 2460, so the sender MUST prefix it with 8 bits of zero when filling the 32-bit field, and the receiver SHOULD ignore those first 8 bits when comparing. The End Flow Label MUST be coded the same way. The TC field follows the same rule as DS in IPv4: 8 bits, with the 6 most significant bits matched and the 2 least significant ignored.
sections.eli5: The IPv6 label is like the IPv4 one with two extras: a tag that marks a conversation, and the type of the next piece of the packet.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The authors have not identified security concerns beyond those already identified in RFC 6089. This document only defines the format of the traffic selector field.

For IANA, the values 1 (IPv4 Binary Traffic Selector) and 2 (IPv6 Binary Traffic Selector) were assigned in the "Traffic Selector Format" namespace for the sub-option defined in RFC 6089.
sections.eli5: This RFC only defines the label layout, so it adds no new safety worries. The old ones still apply.
